questions.question: Explain the nominal/balance-sheet sorting and the meaning carried by the statement's heading.
questions.expected_answer: Nominal accounts (incomes and expenses) measure the year's flows and belong to the Statement of Comprehensive Income; balance sheet accounts (assets, liabilities, capital) measure position at a moment and belong to the Statement of Financial Position. The heading 'for the year ended 28 February' signals a period of accumulated flows, in contrast to 'at 28 February' which signals a moment's position — the prepositions FOR and AT encode the two kinds of account, and an incomplete heading loses marks.

questions.question: Build the statement's three layers with the year's figures, naming each subtotal.
questions.expected_answer: Trading layer: Sales R100 000 (R102 000 less R2 000 debtors allowances) minus Cost of Sales R80 000 gives GROSS PROFIT R20 000. Operating layer: plus other operating income (Rent Income R6 000) gives gross operating income R26 000; minus operating expenses (Salaries R12 000, Telephone R1 200, Insurance R600, Stationery R800, Bank Charges R350, Trading Stock Deficit R150, Depreciation R1 800 — total R16 900) gives OPERATING PROFIT R9 100. Financing layer: plus interest income (none) minus interest expense R1 200 gives NET PROFIT FOR THE YEAR R7 900.

questions.question: Show the workings convention on three adjusted lines and explain the two placement rules the markers watch.
questions.expected_answer: Workings sit in brackets beside the line: Telephone R1 200 (1 100 + 100 owing); Insurance R600 (1 200 − 600 prepaid); Rent Income R6 000 (5 500 + 500 accrued) — so the marker can award the route even if the final figure slips. Placement rules: the trading stock deficit is an operating expense (a surplus would join other operating income), and interest in both directions stays out of the operating block — operating profit must measure the operations alone, with financing framing it from below.
